'''''Hovenia dulcis''''', or the '''oriental raisin tree''', is a hardy tree found in [[Asia]], from Eastern [[China]] ([[wikt:萬壽果|萬壽果]]; pinyin: {{Transliteration|zh|wànshòuguǒ}}) and [[Korea]] ({{lang|ko|헛개나무}}, {{Transliteration|ko|heotgae namu}}) to the [[Himalayas]] (up to altitudes of 2,000 m), growing preferably in a sunny position on moist sandy or loamy soils. The tree known for its health benefits when consumed in tea, introduced as an ornamental tree to several countries, also bears edible fruit. It is considered to be one of the most pervasive invaders in Brazilian subtropical forests.<ref>Cf. Dechoum M, T Castellani, S Zabra, M Rejmànek, N Peronni & J Tamashiro (2014) Community structure, succession and invasibility in a seasonal deciduous forest in southern Brazil. Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Biological Invasions (Neobiota 2014), p. 8.</ref>

== Description ==
[[File:Hovenia dulcis SZ74.png|thumbnail|Hovenia dulcis]]

Tree, rarely a shrub, deciduous, to 10–30 m tall. Branchlets brown or black-purple, [[glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]], with inconspicuous [[lenticel]]s. The glossy leaves are large and pointed. The trees bear clusters of small cream-coloured hermaphroditic flowers in July. The [[drupe]]s appear at the ends of an edible [[rachis]] (fleshy fruit stalk), which is a type of [[accessory fruit]].

== Uses ==
The fleshy rachis of the [[infructescence]] is sweet, fragrant and is edible raw or cooked. Dried, they look and taste like [[raisins]]. An extract of the seeds, bough, and young leaves can be used as a substitute for [[honey]]<ref>{{cite book |last=Facciola |first=Stephen |title=Cornucopia: a source book of edible plants |date=1 November 1990 |publisher=Kampong Publication |isbn=0-9628087-0-9}}</ref> and is used for making wine and candy.

An extract of the [[Leaf|leaves]] contains [[hodulcine]], a [[glycosides|glycoside]] which exhibits an anti-sweet activity.<ref name="Kinghorn-book3">{{cite book |author=Lyn O'Brien Nabors |title=Alternative Sweeteners 3e |date=1 June 2001 |publisher=CRC PressI Llc |isbn=978-0-8247-0437-7}}</ref>

The timber is fine and hard and is used for building construction and fine furniture.

Hovenia dulcis is a natural source for [[dihydromyricetin]], a [[flavonoid]] with antioxidant properties and is primarily found in the tree's leaves, stems, and bark.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.stanfordchem.com/does-dihydromyricetin-dhm-have-any-side-effects.html |title=Does Dihydromyricetin (DHM) Have Any Side Effects? |last=Marchio |first=Cathy |date=4 January 2024 |website=Stanford Chemicals |access-date=5 November 2024}}</ref> It has been used in traditional [[Traditional chinese medicine|Chinese]], [[Traditional Korean medicine|Korean]], and [[Kampo|Japanese]] medicines to treat fever, parasitic infection, as a laxative, and a treatment of liver diseases, and as a [[hangover]] treatment.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Hyun | first1 = TK | display-authors = etal | date = Jul 2010 | title = Hovenia dulcis—an Asian traditional herb | url = | journal = Planta Med. | volume = 76 | issue = 10| pages = 943–9 | pmid = 20379955 | doi = 10.1055/s-0030-1249776 }}</ref> It is also used as medicine for preventing and treating [[Chronic condition|chronic diseases]] as well as skincare products for its ability to protect skin from [[UV]]-induced damage and aging.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wen |first1=Chaoyu |last2=Zhang |first2=Fan |year=2023 |title=Dihydromyricetin alleviates intestinal inflammation by changing intestinal microbial metabolites and inhibiting the expression of the MyD88/NF-κB signaling pathway |journal= Animal Research and One Health|volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=219–232 |doi=10.1002/aro2.21|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite patent |status=patent |country=EP |number=2356980A2}}</ref>

=== Reforestation ===
In Thailand ''Hovenia dulcis'' is relatively rare, typically found in the stream-irrigated valleys of primary lower mountain evergreen forest located between 1,075 and 1,250 metres above sea level. However, it is one of 30 potential species identified as a substitute for ''[[Eucalyptus]] spp''., commonly planted for [[reforestation]], that would meet the demand for rapid growth while not disturbing the ecological balance.<ref name="Sukin">{{Cite web |url=http://reocities.com/rainforest/7813/0206_euc.htm |title=Kamol Sukin "Tropical Feast" |access-date=24 May 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150824024013/http://reocities.com/rainforest/7813/0206_euc.htm |archive-date=24 August 2015 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>[http://www.fao.org/DOCREP/005/AC648E/ac648e0e.htm G. Pakkad, S. Elliott, V. Anusarnsunthorn "FOREST RESTORATION PLANTING IN NORTHERN THAILAND"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190206003454/http://www.fao.org/docrep/005/ac648e/ac648e0e.htm |date=6 February 2019 }} in ''Proceedings of the Southeast Asian Moving Workshop on Conservation, Management and Utilization of Forest Genetic Resources'' 25 February-10 March 2001, Thailand</ref>

In Thailand ''Hovenia dulcis'' grows at roughly the same rate as eucalyptus, reaching six metres in height within three years.<ref name="Sukin" /> One major asset is that the growth form of the tree allows other species to regenerate nearby. Furthermore, the tree is known to attract several varieties both of birds and of mammals which feed on the seeds and fruit.<ref name="FORRU">{{Cite web |url=http://www.siam-society.org/pub_NHB/nhbss_index_v41-50.html |title="The fruits, seeds and seedlings of ''Hovenia dulcis'' Thunb. (Rhamnaceae)." ''Nat. Hist. Bull.''Siam Soc. 44:41–52 1996 |access-date=1 November 2014 |archive-date=1 November 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141101221728/http://www.siam-society.org/pub_NHB/nhbss_index_v41-50.html |url-status=live }}</ref> As well as promoting faunal [[Biodiversity|diversity]], this process assists in improving soil fertility through [[humus|humification]].<ref name="Sukin" />
